title: North Carolina Department of Revenue v. Philip Morris U.S., Inc.
description: Whether the Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) has subject matter jurisdiction over as-applied constitutional challenges to tax statutes, or if such challenges must be dismissed by the OAH and heard by the judicial branch.
plaintiff_argument: Philip Morris argued that N.C. G.S. § 105-241.17 allows the OAH to consider as-applied constitutional challenges to tax statutes, distinguishing them from facial challenges.
defendant_argument: The Department of Revenue argued that the OAH lacks subject matter jurisdiction over any constitutional challenges to tax statutes, whether facial or as-applied, and that such jurisdiction is reserved for the judicial branch.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Business Court's decision, ruling that N.C. G.S. § 105-241.17 does not grant the OAH subject matter jurisdiction over as-applied constitutional challenges to tax statutes, and therefore the OAH lacked jurisdiction over Philip Morris's petition.

title: State v. Rogers
description: Whether the good faith exception to the exclusionary rule applies to cell-site location information (CSLI) obtained under an order later found to lack probable cause, and whether North Carolina's state constitution includes a good faith exception to its exclusionary rule.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the statutory good faith exception under N.C.G.S. § 15A-974 applies, and that the Court should overrule State v. Carter to adopt a good faith exception for the state constitution, making the CSLI admissible.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the CSLI was obtained in violation of his constitutional rights, and the good faith exception should not apply because the officer's reliance on the order was objectively unreasonable, thus the evidence should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, upholding the trial court's denial of the defendant's motion to suppress, thereby allowing the cell-site location information (CSLI) to be admitted as evidence.

title: Mohebali v. Hayes
description: Whether a legislative cap imposed by the trial judge on noneconomic damages awarded by the jury in a medical malpractice action violates the plaintiff's right to a jury trial under Article I, Section 25 of the North Carolina Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that the legislative cap on noneconomic damages is unconstitutional, violating her right to a jury trial.
defendant_argument: The defendant (supported by amicus curiae) argues that the legislative cap is constitutional and does not violate the right to a jury trial.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision to apply the Legislative Cap, concluding that the cap is constitutional and does not violate the plaintiff's right to a jury trial.

title: State v. Kelliher
description: Whether a resentencing court, following a mandate to impose concurrent life sentences for murder convictions, retains de novo authority to determine if ancillary robbery and conspiracy sentences should run consecutively or concurrently.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Court of Appeals erred by limiting the resentencing court's discretion, asserting that N.C.G.S. § 15A-1354(a) grants trial courts de novo resentencing authority for all convictions, including ancillary ones, as long as the overall sentence complies with the previous mandate.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the resentencing court exceeded its authority under the Kelliher I mandate, which only addressed the murder convictions, and therefore lacked jurisdiction to impose consecutive sentences for the ancillary robbery and conspiracy convictions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and reinstated the resentencing court's 31 March 2023 judgments, which included consecutive sentences for robbery and conspiracy.

title: State of North Carolina v. Chambers
description: Whether a statute that allows a juror to be excused and substituted by an alternate after the jury in a criminal trial has begun to deliberate violates the state constitutional right to a twelve-person jury.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the statute allowing mid-deliberation juror substitution is constitutional, especially with the instruction to restart deliberations, and that the defendant waived his challenge by not objecting at trial.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court's substitution of an alternate juror during deliberations violated his state constitutional right to a twelve-person jury.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, holding that the statute allowing mid-deliberation juror substitution with an instruction to restart deliberations does not violate the state constitutional right to a jury of twelve.

title: Howell v. Cooper; North Carolina Bar and Tavern Association v. Stein
description: Whether Governor Cooper's executive orders, which restricted the operation of bars during the COVID-19 pandemic while allowing other businesses to reopen, violated the plaintiffs' constitutional rights under the Fruits of Labor and Equal Protection Clauses, and statutory rights under the Emergency Management Act and Public Records Act.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Governor's executive orders arbitrarily singled out bars for closure, denying them the fundamental right to earn a living without sufficient public health justification, and violated statutory provisions.
defendant_argument: The Governor argued that the executive orders were reasonable, data-driven responses to a public health emergency, necessary to slow COVID-19 spread, and that sovereign immunity precluded the plaintiffs' constitutional claims, while statutory claims lacked merit.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court modified and affirmed in part the Court of Appeals' decision to vacate the trial court's summary judgment on the Fruits of Labor claim, remanding it for further factual discovery under the correct legal standard. The Court reversed the Court of Appeals' application of strict scrutiny to the Equal Protection claim, affirming that rational basis review is the proper standard for economic regulations. The Court also affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision to dismiss the plaintiffs' statutory claims under the Emergency Management Act and Public Records Act.

title: Happel v. Board of Education
description: Whether the Public Readiness and Emergency Preparedness (PREP) Act immunizes state actors who forcibly vaccinate a child without consent, thereby committing battery and infringing fundamental state constitutional rights.
plaintiff_argument: The PREP Act does not immunize defendants from claims of battery and violations of state constitutional rights, as it does not preempt state constitutional claims.
defendant_argument: The PREP Act completely immunizes them from the plaintiffs' suit because it preempts all state law claims, including battery and state constitutional rights violations.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the dismissal of the battery claim but reversed the dismissal of the state constitutional claims, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: North Carolina NAACP v. Moore
description: Whether legislators elected from unconstitutionally racially gerrymandered districts possess the authority to initiate the process of changing the North Carolina Constitution by proposing constitutional amendments.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the General Assembly, being illegally composed of legislators elected from unconstitutionally gerrymandered districts, lacked the legitimate authority to propose constitutional amendments, viewing these legislators as 'usurpers' whose actions should be void.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the legislators, even if elected from unconstitutionally gerrymandered districts, were at a minimum 'de facto officers' and retained full legislative authority, and that invalidating their actions would cause chaos and confusion without a principled distinction between types of legislative acts.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, which had reversed the trial court's order declaring the Voter ID and Tax Cap Amendments void, and remanded the case to the superior court for further proceedings to determine if the amendments should be invalidated based on specific criteria.

title: Griffin v. State Board of Elections
description: Whether the North Carolina State Board of Elections properly dismissed election protests challenging votes based on incomplete voter registrations, lack of photo identification for military and overseas voters, and the eligibility of "Never Residents".
plaintiff_argument: Jefferson Griffin argued that the Board erred in dismissing his election protests, contending that voters with incomplete registrations, military and overseas voters without photo ID, and "Never Residents" were not lawfully registered or eligible to vote, and that the Board's notice requirements conflicted with state law.
defendant_argument: The North Carolina State Board of Elections argued that Griffin's protests were properly dismissed due to inadequate notice and failure to establish probable cause of election law violations, asserting that its procedures for voter registration and absentee voting, including for military, overseas, and "Never Resident" voters, were lawful.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed the Superior Court's affirmation of the Board's dismissal of Griffin's protests, remanding the cases with instructions to allow a 15-day cure period for voters with incomplete registrations and photo ID issues, and to remove "Never Resident" votes from the final count.

title: State v. Francisco Edgar Tirado
description: Whether the Court of Appeals denied merits review of the defendant's constitutional challenge to his consecutive life without parole sentences under Article I, Section 27 of the North Carolina Constitution, and whether that state constitution provides broader protections than the Eighth Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Court of Appeals comprehensively addressed all of the defendant's arguments, including his constitutional challenge, and that Article I, Section 27 of the state constitution provides less protection than the Eighth Amendment, thus affirming the lower court's decision.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Court of Appeals failed to provide merits review of his constitutional challenge to his consecutive life without parole sentences under Article I, Section 27 of the North Carolina Constitution, which he contended offers broader protections than the Eighth Amendment.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals, upholding the defendant's consecutive sentences of life imprisonment without parole.

title: In re Chastain
description: Whether a replacement judge has the constitutional authority to preside over the removal of an elected clerk of superior court when the senior resident judge is recused, whether procedural due process requires that removal be based solely on allegations in the initiating sworn affidavit, and what the proper constitutional standard for removal of a clerk is under Article IV.
plaintiff_argument: Ms. Chastain argued that the replacement judge lacked authority, that the removal orders improperly considered allegations not in the initial affidavit, and that her conduct did not meet the standard for removal.
defendant_argument: Mr. Thompson, who initiated the removal inquiry, sought Ms. Chastain's removal based on alleged misconduct, arguing that the removal was proper.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' decision, overruled a prior holding, and remanded the case, clarifying that a replacement judge has authority, removal must be based only on initial affidavit allegations, and the standard is "misconduct."

title: Mitchell v. University of North Carolina Board of Governors
description: Whether North Carolina courts should apply de novo review or defer to a state agency's interpretation of its own rules and regulations.
plaintiff_argument: Dr. Mitchell argued that the University failed to follow its own rules and regulations in dismissing him and that his letter containing racial slurs was protected First Amendment speech.
defendant_argument: The University argued that it complied with its Handbook procedures for dismissal and that Dr. Mitchell's letter was not protected First Amendment speech.
decision_outcome: The court modified and affirmed the Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that state courts must apply de novo review to state agency interpretations of regulations and rejecting the dissent's argument for remanding the First Amendment issue.

title: McKinney v. Goins
description: Whether the expiration of a tort claim's statute of limitations creates a constitutionally protected vested right, thereby limiting the legislature's authority to retroactively revive previously expired tort claims.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the SAFE Child Act is constitutional because the running of a statute of limitations does not create a vested right, and the legislature has the authority to retroactively alter procedural remedies.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the expiration of a tort claim's statute of limitations creates a constitutionally protected vested right under the Law of the Land Clause, which is immune from legislative interference.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the SAFE Child Act is constitutional and that there is no constitutionally protected vested right in the running of a tort claim's statute of limitations.

title: Askew v. City of Kinston
description: Whether plaintiffs bringing Corum claims must exhaust administrative remedies before entering the courthouse doors.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argue that administrative exhaustion is not a jurisdictional prerequisite for Corum claims, especially when the administrative process cannot adequately address systemic racial discrimination and arbitrary property condemnation.
defendant_argument: Defendant argued that plaintiffs failed to exhaust administrative remedies, which is a jurisdictional prerequisite for Corum claims.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that administrative exhaustion does not dictate jurisdiction over Corum claims, and remanded the case for a review on the merits.

title: Fearrington v. City of Greenville
description: Whether the City of Greenville's Red Light Camera Enforcement Program (RLCEP) and its funding mechanism, authorized by a Local Act and Interlocal Agreement, violate North Carolina's Fines and Forfeitures Clause (FFC) and N.C. G.S. § 115C-437 by allocating less than 90% of collected penalties to public schools.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the RLCEP's funding mechanism violated the FFC and N.C. G.S. § 115C-437 by diverting 'clear proceeds' of red light fines away from Pitt County public schools, as the Board received less than the statutorily required 90% of collected penalties.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Local Act specifically authorized the cost-sharing agreement, exempting them from the 10% cap, and that the program, by providing a revenue stream to schools that would otherwise not exist, aligns with the FFC's purpose.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the plaintiffs' taxpayer standing but reversed the Court of Appeals' decision on the FFC challenge, ruling that the Interlocal Agreement and Local Act do not plainly and clearly violate the FFC's text or purpose, and remanded for summary judgment in favor of Greenville and the Board.

title: Bouvier v. Porter
description: Whether the absolute privilege from defamation claims applies broadly to all individuals involved in election protests, or if it requires direct participation in quasi-judicial proceedings.
plaintiff_argument: The absolute privilege should be narrowly applied, only protecting statements made by direct participants (parties, counsel, witnesses) in judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings.
defendant_argument: The absolute privilege should broadly protect all individuals involved in any aspect of election protests, as the privilege belongs to the occasion of the proceeding, not the individual's role.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the absolute privilege broadly protects all individuals involved in election protests from defamation claims, and remanded the case for dismissal with prejudice.

title: Washington v. Cline
description: Whether the dismissal of criminal charges for a speedy trial violation constitutes an adequate remedy under the Corum doctrine, thereby precluding a separate civil claim for money damages against the State.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that vacating his criminal convictions for a speedy trial violation was not an adequate remedy and he should also receive money damages from the State for the constitutional violation under a Corum claim.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the dismissal of criminal charges for a speedy trial violation was an adequate remedy, and therefore, a Corum claim for money damages is not available.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that the plaintiff's Corum claim for money damages was barred because the dismissal of his criminal charges constituted an adequate alternative remedy for the speedy trial violation.

title: Holmes v. Moore
description: Whether S.B. 824, a voter identification law, violates Article I, Section 19 of the North Carolina Constitution by being enacted with discriminatory intent and producing a meaningful disparate impact along racial lines.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argue S.B. 824 violates Article I, Section 19 of the North Carolina Constitution due to discriminatory intent and its burden on the fundamental right to vote, creating disparate classes of voters, infringing on free elections, conditioning voting on property, and infringing on rights of assembly, petition, and free speech.
defendant_argument: Defendants argue S.B. 824 is constitutional, was not enacted with discriminatory intent, does not produce a meaningful disparate impact, and is one of the least restrictive voter identification laws.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's judgment and remanded the case for dismissal of the plaintiffs' claim with prejudice.

title: Community Success Initiative v. Moore
description: Whether N.C. G.S. § 13-1, which requires felons to complete their sentences, including probation, parole, or post-release supervision and financial obligations, before regaining voting rights, is unconstitutional due to racial discrimination, wealth-based classification, or violation of the Free Elections Clause.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that N.C. G.S. § 13-1 is unconstitutional because it discriminates against African Americans in intent and effect, creates an impermissible wealth-based classification, and violates the Free Elections Clause by preventing elections that accurately reflect the will of the people.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued that N.C. G.S. § 13-1 is constitutional, that the trial court misapplied the law and overlooked facts, and that the statute was not motivated by racial discrimination. They also contended that felons do not have a fundamental right to vote and the law does not create an impermissible wealth classification.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's judgment, ruling that N.C. G.S. § 13-1 is constitutional and does not violate the North Carolina Constitution.

title: Harper v. Hall
description: Whether the North Carolina Constitution prohibits partisan gerrymandering, with plaintiffs arguing it violates constitutional provisions and defendants arguing such claims are nonjusticiable political questions.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that legislative and congressional redistricting plans constituted unconstitutional partisan gerrymanders, violating the state constitution's free elections, equal protection, free speech, and freedom of assembly clauses, and engaged in racial vote dilution.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued that partisan gerrymandering claims are nonjusticiable political questions, as the state constitution assigns redistricting authority to the General Assembly, lacks judicially manageable standards for such claims, and does not explicitly prohibit partisan gerrymandering.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that partisan gerrymandering claims are nonjusticiable political questions under the North Carolina Constitution, overruling previous decisions (Harper I and Harper II) that held them justiciable, and dismissed all plaintiffs' claims with prejudice.

title: State v. Rollinson
description: Whether the Court of Appeals erred by concluding that the trial court complied with the statutory procedure for obtaining the defendant's waiver of his right to a jury trial for the status offense of habitual felon, where the defendant argues the court did not personally address him sufficiently, and the State argues the procedure was followed.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the trial court complied with N.C. G.S. § 15A-1201(d)(1) because the statutory language does not prohibit a defendant from responding through counsel regarding the waiver of a jury trial.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that to "address the defendant personally" and determine understanding of the waiver consequences, the defendant himself must respond to the trial court's address, and counsel responding on his behalf is insufficient.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, concluding that the trial court complied with the statutory procedure for obtaining the defendant's waiver of his right to a jury trial for the habitual felon offense.

title: State v. Diaz-Tomas
description: Whether a criminal defendant possesses the right to compel the district attorney to reinstate dismissed criminal charges and place them on a trial court's calendar, and whether the Superior Court properly denied the defendant's petition for writ of certiorari.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the district attorney has exclusive and discretionary power to reinstate criminal charges, and that trial courts lack the authority to compel such reinstatement, as doing so would infringe upon the district attorney's constitutional and statutory duties.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued he has a right to compel the reinstatement of his dismissed criminal charges and to have them placed on a trial court's calendar for disposition, and that the Superior Court erred in denying his petition for writ of certiorari.
decision_outcome: The Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that a criminal defendant does not possess the right to compel the district attorney to reinstate dismissed criminal charges, and a trial court lacks the authority to order such reinstatement.

title: State v. Hamer
description: Whether the trial court's initial noncompliance with statutory procedures for waiving a jury trial constituted structural error, thereby invalidating the defendant's waiver of his constitutional right to a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that despite initial procedural noncompliance, the trial court remedied the error, and the defendant knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to a jury trial without prejudice.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court's failure to follow the statutorily prescribed procedure for jury trial waiver constituted structural error, meaning he did not knowingly and voluntarily waive his right, and thus a new trial is required.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction for speeding, ruling that the trial court remedied any initial procedural error and the defendant validly waived his right to a jury trial.

title: Deminski v. State Board of Education
description: Whether an individual may bring a claim under the North Carolina Constitution for a school board's deliberate indifference to continual student harassment that denies students their constitutionally guaranteed right to a sound basic education, with the plaintiff arguing such a claim is permissible and the defendant arguing it is barred by governmental immunity.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that the defendant's deliberate indifference to ongoing student harassment denied the plaintiff-students their constitutional right to a sound basic education, and this constitutes a colorable claim not barred by governmental immunity.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the constitutional claim is barred by the defense of sovereign or governmental immunity and should be dismissed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the trial court correctly denied the defendant's motion to dismiss, thereby allowing the plaintiff's constitutional claim to proceed.

title: Cheryl Lloyd Humphrey Land Inv. Co. v. Resco Products, Inc.
description: Whether defendants' statements made during public rezoning hearings are protected petitioning activity under the First Amendment and state constitution, thereby granting immunity from a lawsuit alleging tortious interference.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the defendants' intentional and malicious misrepresentations made to the Town of Hillsborough were not protected speech and tortiously interfered with the plaintiff's prospective economic advantage, causing Braddock Park Homes, Inc. to not purchase the property.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that their statements made at public rezoning hearings were constitutionally protected petitioning activity under the First Amendment and Article I, Section 12 of the North Carolina Constitution, granting them immunity from the lawsuit.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, thereby upholding the trial court's dismissal of the plaintiff's lawsuit against the defendants.
